and to get around that people have developed personal and private benchmark suites that reflect their own workloads, much like the proposed pie-filling-cost test.

I'd wager a guess that your grandma baked pies.

My grandmother used blueberry pie filling for her benchmark of "is this store cheaper than that grocery store?"

One store has four brands that range from $2.99 (on sale from $3.29) to $7.99 (on sale from $9.59). Another nearby store has a single brand at $9.49 that's marked as local.

Given this information, which store likely has the less expensive food?

Furthermore, it was her marker for inflation - she knew what blueberry pie filling cost the previous month, the previous year, ... and many previous years to that.

She lived in a small town in the rural south that had a general store - any grocery store was a forty minute to two hour drive away...

It was a consistent thing that she could track and measure across the months and decades and compare when shopping (is this a store that I get only the essentials for the next week or is this a store that I should stock up on and come back to?).

So too is the pelican, or the raccoon with a radio in a where's Waldo style drawing. It's something to measure across models that is consistent.

Fortunately, none of the stores caught onto my grandmother's preference for blueberry pie filling.

One might worry about pelican maxing... or raccoon maxing... and Goodhart's law gets into the question of "do LLM testers use that for testing too?"
Not sure this is a good way to benchmark LLM's, no offence, but a single SVG is hardly a measure of a models capability.

children.author: viraptor
children.text: To be fair, people have a genuine preference for images with things facing to the right. And lots of drawings will do 3 motion lines. You'd likely draw a dashed rather than solid separator too, or it would look like a random line. Lots of the AI habits are there because of choices we make.

Same reason they're all facing right with the same composition, they all have three motion lines, they all have a yellow sun and 2-3 blobby clouds, they're all on two-lane pavement with a white dashed lane separator.

And the same reason Claude has all its notorious Claudisms in prose.

The shorter and vaguer a prompt you give to an LLM, the more it fills in further details using associations they've developed through training. These are ley lines that the models gravitate towards. Diffusion models too.

It's why lazy AI use for creative work always comes across as lazy in the wild and always will.

When you use AI for "creative" purposes yourself, it feels like magic to see a pelican riding a bicycle at all, and you're impressed by all those cool details it added. But then 10, or 100, or 10M people throw more or less the same trivial prompts at it and we start to recognize all those "ley line" associations fill in the gaps the same way again and again and again.

children.author: GuB-42
children.text:
Human lawyers, coders, accountants and designers are a lot more than their jobs.

They are people with common knowledge, a lawyer has to understand carpentry to understand how to deal with how a client's roof fell off, a coder has to understand transportation for writing a travel app, an accountant has to understand medicine to do accounting for a pharmacy, a designer has to understand cooking to design a toaster. Not expert knowledge, but enough to understand that toasters are hot and need electricity.

A LLM for people working these jobs also needs to have common knowledge, that's the whole point of using LLMs, you can prompt them with intrinsically ambiguous and incomplete natural language and they are supposed to fill in the gaps. And the more common knowledge they have, the better they are at it. So why settle for less? If it is an optimization problem, we already have the solution, it is the "mixture of experts", which is better at optimizing then having an "lawyer LLM", "coder LLM", etc... because it is better adapted to the internal structure of the neural network behind it.

children.author: ProblemExplorer
dvaplima
children.text: thanks for the compilation of benchmarks

Meta seems to have designed Ember to be a strong "all round" great value model - it dominates most of its class on cost

The noncoding results on some reports grabbed my attention. Ember also looks like a particularly inexpensive option for some agent workflows.

On Artificial Analysis, Ember max scored 36 on the Intelligence Index at ~$0.14 per task, compared with 35 at $8 for Grok 4.7 xhigh, and 28 at $0.15 for GPT-6 Luna max. Haiku 5.5 max also scores 36, at $0.41 per task. These are AA's measured costs across its index for those specific configurations.

That puts Ember in roughly Grok's aggregate score range at about 1/55 of the measured cost, and ahead of Luna at a similar cost! [1]

The Vals finance/legal results are also particularly interesting: comparing Ember with GPT-6.1 Terra, both evaluated at "max" reasoning:

- Finance Agent v2.1: 63.83% vs 55.96%, at $0.06 vs $1.92 (!) per test. [2]

- Legal Research Bench: 49.04% vs 25.96%, at $0.06 vs $3.22 (!) per test. [3]

- HLAB-Vals-1.1: 25% vs 1.67%, at $0.12 vs $1.48 (!) per test. [4]

Those are INSANE score differences, at roughly 1/32, 1/54 and 1/12 of Terra's respective benchmark costs!

Misleadingly, their overall Vals Index scores are almost identical: 60.48% for Ember and 60.54% for Terra. Terra also scores higher on Vals' Terminal-Bench 4.0 run: 49.49% vs 39.39%. They arrive at similar aggregate scores through quite different strengths. [5][6]

For me, this reinforces the case for custom, workload specific evals. Broad benchmarks have been useful for shortlisting models but choosing between them, calls for representative tasks, explicit success criteria and measurements using the tools and reasoning settings you actually intend to deploy.

I certainly want to measure cost per successfully completed task, including retries and escalation.

Reusing a framework such as Harbor with a custom task suite seems increasingly useful here. [7] The aggregate score here gives me a starting point but the tasks I actually need done then determines my choice.

Goign by the generic benchmarks would confuse me to no end and likely burn me out.

Great times to be in!

[1] https://artificialanalysis.ai/leaderboards/models

[2] https://www.vals.ai/benchmarks/fabv2-1

[3] https://www.vals.ai/benchmarks/legal_research

[4] https://www.vals.ai/benchmarks/hlab

[5] https://www.vals.ai/models/meta_muse-ember

[6] https://www.vals.ai/models/openai_gpt-6.1-terra

[7] https://github.com/harbor-framework/harbor
